weeks.title: Week 1: The Journey Begins
weeks.babyDevelopment: Conception hasn't happened yet — this is when pregnancy dating begins, counting from the first day of your partner's last period. Her body is priming for ovulation as hormone levels shift, building the uterine lining and preparing to release an egg. Everything that happens over the next 40 weeks starts here.
weeks.partnerExperience: Your partner may not know she's pregnant yet, and technically, she isn't — but her body is already entering the pre-ovulation phase. She may notice some mild hormonal shifts, but most women feel completely normal during this time. The journey has quietly begun.
howToHelp: Start taking prenatal vitamins together
Discuss family planning and readiness
Begin tracking her cycle if trying to conceive

actionItems.text: Research prenatal vitamins and start taking them
Have a conversation about parenting goals

weeks.commonDadQuestion: Is this really happening?
weeks.commonDadAnswer: Yes — and it's completely normal to feel a mix of excitement and disbelief. Give yourself time to process. Many dads don't feel it's real until they hear the heartbeat or see the first ultrasound.

weeks.title: Week 2: Conception Window
weeks.babyDevelopment: Ovulation occurs and fertilization may happen during this narrow window. A single sperm penetrates the egg to form a zygote — a brand new cell containing a unique combination of DNA that determines your baby's traits, sex, and genetic blueprint. All 46 chromosomes that define this person are set in this single moment.
weeks.partnerExperience: Your partner may notice signs of ovulation: a slight rise in basal body temperature, mild cramping, or changes in cervical mucus. This is the most fertile window of her cycle, and the opportunity is brief — typically just 12 to 24 hours after ovulation.
howToHelp: Be supportive and reduce stress at home
Avoid alcohol and smoking
Keep communication open about the process

actionItems.text: Remove alcohol from the house to support her
Learn about the conception process

weeks.title: Week 3: Implantation
weeks.babyDevelopment: The fertilized egg — now a rapidly dividing cluster of cells called a blastocyst — travels down the fallopian tube and burrows into the uterine wall in a process called implantation. Cell division is happening at an extraordinary pace, and the outer cells are beginning to form what will become the placenta. This is the first physical connection between your baby and your partner's body.
weeks.partnerExperience: Some women experience light spotting or mild cramping around implantation, which can easily be mistaken for the start of a period. Most women feel nothing at all and have no idea this remarkable moment is unfolding inside them. The body is keeping this secret quietly.
howToHelp: Stay calm if there's light spotting — it can be normal
Encourage her to avoid caffeine
Start reading about early pregnancy together

actionItems.text: Stock up on pregnancy-friendly snacks
Research local OB-GYNs or midwives

weeks.title: Week 4: Positive Test
weeks.babyDevelopment: The embryo is about 2mm long — smaller than a grain of rice. The amniotic sac and early placenta are beginning to take shape, and the embryo is already dividing into three distinct layers that will eventually become all of the body's organs, muscles, and skin. The foundational architecture of a human being is quietly assembling itself.
weeks.partnerExperience: A missed period and a positive pregnancy test mark this week for many women. Fatigue may be the first noticeable symptom — the body is working overtime to establish the pregnancy, and surging progesterone levels often feel like a wave of exhaustion that hits out of nowhere.
howToHelp: Be present when she takes the test
Celebrate the news together before telling others
Schedule the first prenatal visit

actionItems.text: Schedule the first prenatal appointment
Discuss when and how to share the news

weeks.commonDadQuestion: When do we tell people?
weeks.commonDadAnswer: Most couples wait until after week 12-13 when miscarriage risk drops significantly. Until then, only tell people you'd want supporting you regardless of outcome.

weeks.title: Week 5: Heart Begins Beating
weeks.babyDevelopment: The neural tube — the structure that will become the brain and spinal cord — is forming, which is why folic acid is so critical in these early weeks. A tiny heart has started pulsing at around 110 beats per minute, circulating blood through a rudimentary vascular system. It's the first organ to function, and that rhythmic beat marks one of the most profound moments in early development.
weeks.partnerExperience: Nausea often strikes for the first time this week, sometimes before your partner even knows she's pregnant. Fatigue can be overwhelming, breasts may feel tender and sore, and a heightened sense of smell is common — all signs that pregnancy hormones are surging through her body and doing exactly what they're supposed to.
howToHelp: Stock nausea-friendly foods like crackers and ginger tea
Take over heavier household chores
Be patient with mood changes

actionItems.text: Stock the kitchen with nausea-friendly snacks
Research what to expect at the first prenatal visit

weeks.commonDadQuestion: Is morning sickness normal?
weeks.commonDadAnswer: Very — up to 80% of pregnant women experience it, and it can hit any time of day. It usually peaks around weeks 8-10 and fades by week 14. Keep bland snacks on hand and help manage her triggers.

weeks.title: Week 6: Arms and Legs Budding
weeks.babyDevelopment: Tiny arm and leg buds are emerging from the sides of the embryo, and blood is beginning to circulate through a basic vascular system. Early structures for the ears, eyes, nose, and mouth are also forming — though they look like small bumps and pits at this stage, every detail is precisely mapped out in the growing embryo's cells.
weeks.partnerExperience: Morning sickness may be intensifying, and despite its name, it can arrive at any hour of the day or night. Heightened smell sensitivity becomes a major trigger for many women — foods, perfumes, and household scents that were once enjoyable can suddenly provoke immediate nausea.
howToHelp: Take over cooking to reduce smell triggers
Keep a trash bag nearby in the car just in case
Be understanding — this phase is temporary

actionItems.text: Take over cooking duties this week
Identify her nausea triggers and eliminate them

weeks.commonDadQuestion: What if she can't keep food down?
weeks.commonDadAnswer: Try small frequent meals — crackers, ginger, cold foods, and bland options often help. If she can't hold down fluids for 24+ hours or is losing weight, call her OB. Severe nausea can need medical treatment.

weeks.title: Week 7: Brain Growing Fast
weeks.babyDevelopment: The brain is developing at a remarkable pace, generating roughly 100 new neurons every minute. Cartilage is beginning to form throughout the body, and while the hands and feet are still paddle-shaped, the digits are starting to separate. The embryo is growing about a millimeter each day.
weeks.partnerExperience: Nausea is often at its peak this week, and extreme fatigue can make it hard for her to keep up with daily life. Emotional sensitivity is heightened too — she may swing between excitement and dread, and both feelings are completely valid and worth acknowledging.
howToHelp: Let her rest without guilt
Handle more of the daily tasks
Avoid strong colognes or scents that trigger nausea

actionItems.text: Help identify and reduce nausea triggers at home
Prepare a list of questions for the first prenatal appointment

weeks.commonDadQuestion: Should we see a doctor about the nausea?
weeks.commonDadAnswer: Nausea is normal, but call the OB if she's losing weight, can't keep fluids down, or feels dizzy. There are safe prescription options — there's no reason she has to suffer through it.

weeks.title: Week 8: First Prenatal Visit
weeks.babyDevelopment: All major organ systems — heart, brain, lungs, kidneys, liver — are forming and beginning to function. The umbilical cord is fully formed and actively delivering nutrients and oxygen to the growing embryo. At about half an inch long, an ultrasound this week can show a steady, visible heartbeat — often the first moment it truly feels real.
weeks.partnerExperience: Nausea and fatigue are continuing to peak for most women around this time. Frequent urination is becoming hard to ignore as the growing uterus puts pressure on the bladder — and this is really just the beginning of what will be a long stretch of bathroom trips throughout the pregnancy.
howToHelp: Attend the first prenatal visit — don't miss this one
Ask questions and take notes
Be her advocate in the doctor's office

actionItems.text: Attend the first prenatal appointment
Review your health insurance coverage for pregnancy

weeks.commonDadQuestion: What if we miscarry?
weeks.commonDadAnswer: About 10-15% of known pregnancies end in miscarriage, most in the first trimester. If it happens, it's not her fault or yours. Allow space for grief, lean on each other, and talk to the OB — many couples go on to have healthy pregnancies.

weeks.title: Week 9: Tiny Features Forming
weeks.babyDevelopment: This week marks an important milestone: the embryo officially graduates to fetus. Tiny tooth buds are forming beneath the gums, taste buds are developing, and toes are becoming distinctly visible as the digits fully separate. The fetus is about an inch long and looks recognizably human for the first time.
weeks.partnerExperience: Frequent urination, bloating, and gas remain constant companions as the digestive system slows under the influence of progesterone. Emotionally, she may feel more anxious or sensitive as the full reality of what's happening sinks in — open, gentle communication makes a bigger difference than you might expect.
howToHelp: Review health insurance options together
Start thinking about your budget for baby costs
Keep being patient with the physical discomforts

actionItems.text: Review health insurance and understand your coverage
Start a baby budget spreadsheet

weeks.commonDadQuestion: Can we afford this?
weeks.commonDadAnswer: Most parents feel this way. Start by reviewing your budget and identifying savings. The biggest costs are childcare and parental leave — plan for those first. Many baby items can be borrowed or bought secondhand.

weeks.title: Week 10: Fingers and Toes
weeks.babyDevelopment: Fingers and toes are now fully separated and clearly defined. The baby is making small spontaneous movements, though they're far too faint to feel from outside. All vital organs are formed and beginning to function, with the heart beating at around 170 beats per minute — nearly twice the resting adult rate.
weeks.partnerExperience: Nausea may begin to ease slightly for some women this week, though it lingers strongly for others. Hormonal fluctuations continue to drive emotional swings — what she needs most right now is patient, consistent support rather than attempts to fix how she's feeling.
howToHelp: Research genetic testing options available at week 10-12
Keep the mood at home calm and supportive
Plan a low-key date night to connect

actionItems.text: Research genetic testing options with your partner
Plan a relaxed date night this week

weeks.commonDadQuestion: Are genetic tests necessary?
weeks.commonDadAnswer: Not required, but worth considering. Tests like the NIPT screen for chromosomal conditions with no risk to the baby and can reveal the sex. Talk to her OB about what makes sense for you.

weeks.title: Week 11: Baby Opens Fists
weeks.babyDevelopment: The baby is opening and closing its tiny fists, and may already be hiccupping — though you won't feel a thing yet. Tooth buds are forming under the gums in preparation for baby teeth that won't arrive for months after birth. The ears are also shifting toward their final position on the sides of the head.
weeks.partnerExperience: Bloating and gas remain common as progesterone continues to slow digestion. The good news is that energy levels often begin a slow and welcome return this week — some women notice a genuine shift out of the first-trimester fog, even if nausea isn't fully gone yet.
howToHelp: Start researching daycare options — waitlists can be long
Look into parental leave policies at your job
Keep up with household tasks

actionItems.text: Start researching daycare options and waitlists
Review your company's paternity leave policy

weeks.commonDadQuestion: Is it too early to plan childcare?
weeks.commonDadAnswer: Actually, now is the right time. Infant daycare waitlists can be 6-12+ months in many cities. Start researching options now — daycare centers, nannies, family care — so you're not scrambling later.

weeks.title: Week 12: All Organs Present
weeks.babyDevelopment: All major organs are present and beginning to work together. At about 3 inches long — roughly the size of a lime — the baby has a fully formed face, functioning kidneys, and a beating heart that your OB can detect clearly on a Doppler. The risk of miscarriage drops significantly after this point, making it one of the most meaningful milestones of the first trimester.
weeks.partnerExperience: Energy is returning for many women as the worst of the first-trimester symptoms begin to fade. Nausea often eases noticeably, and the emotional heaviness that marks early pregnancy can start to lift — this can feel like coming up for air after weeks of barely keeping it together.
howToHelp: Plan how and when to announce the pregnancy
Celebrate making it to the end of the first trimester
Start thinking about the nursery

actionItems.text: Plan your pregnancy announcement
Celebrate the end of the first trimester together

weeks.commonDadQuestion: When is it safe to share the news?
weeks.commonDadAnswer: Most couples share after week 12, when miscarriage risk drops to about 1%. But there's no rule. Some share earlier with close family, others wait until the anatomy scan. Do what feels right for you both.

weeks.title: Week 13: End of First Trimester
weeks.babyDevelopment: Vocal cords are beginning to form, and the fingerprints that will be uniquely your baby's are developing in the ridges of the fingertips. The fetus is now swallowing amniotic fluid and practicing the reflexes it will rely on after birth — rooting, sucking, and even reacting to touch and stimulation.
weeks.partnerExperience: Appetite is returning as nausea fades for most women by the end of this week. She likely feels more like herself — more energy, more appetite, and a real sense of emotional relief now that the highest-risk phase of pregnancy is behind you both.
howToHelp: Notify your employer and begin planning paternity leave
Share the news with family and close friends
Start reading a pregnancy book together

actionItems.text: Notify your employer and start planning paternity leave
Share the news with family and friends

weeks.commonDadQuestion: How do I tell my boss?
weeks.commonDadAnswer: You're not required to tell your employer until closer to leave. When you do, share your expected leave dates and any coverage needs. Review your company's parental leave policy now so there are no surprises.

weeks.title: Week 14: Second Trimester Starts
weeks.babyDevelopment: Fingerprints are permanently forming in the ridges of the baby's fingertips. The baby is developing the ability to make subtle facial expressions — squinting, frowning — as the facial muscles grow and connect to the brain. The kidneys are now producing urine, which gets recycled into the amniotic fluid the baby practices swallowing.
weeks.partnerExperience: Round ligament pain — sharp twinges or a dull ache in the lower abdomen or sides — may begin as the uterus expands and the ligaments that support it are forced to stretch. Energy is generally much better in the second trimester, and many women describe this period as the most comfortable stretch of the whole pregnancy.
howToHelp: Share the pregnancy news with your wider circle
Start thinking about the baby registry
Ask about her physical discomforts and how to help

actionItems.text: Share the pregnancy news with coworkers and extended family
Begin researching what to put on the baby registry

weeks.commonDadQuestion: Why does her side hurt?
weeks.commonDadAnswer: Round ligament pain — totally normal. As the uterus grows, the ligaments supporting it stretch, causing sharp or aching pain in the lower abdomen or sides. It peaks in the second trimester and isn't harmful.

weeks.title: Week 15: Lungs Developing
weeks.babyDevelopment: The baby's lungs are developing rapidly, and it's already practicing the breathing motions it will need at birth — inhaling and exhaling amniotic fluid to strengthen the lungs and develop the muscles involved in breathing. Taste buds are also maturing, and the baby can now detect different flavors in the amniotic fluid, which is influenced by what your partner eats.
weeks.partnerExperience: Nasal congestion is a surprisingly common pregnancy symptom at this stage, caused by increased blood volume and swelling in the nasal passages — a condition sometimes called pregnancy rhinitis. Energy levels are usually much better now, and many women feel genuinely good during the middle weeks of the second trimester.
howToHelp: Start the baby registry together
Research strollers, car seats, and essentials
Check in on how she's feeling emotionally

actionItems.text: Create your baby registry
Research car seat safety ratings

weeks.commonDadQuestion: What do we actually need to buy?
weeks.commonDadAnswer: The true essentials are a safe sleep surface, car seat, diapers, onesies, and feeding supplies. Skip the rest for now — many 'must-have' items aren't. You'll figure out what you actually need after baby arrives.

weeks.title: Week 16: Baby Can Hear
weeks.babyDevelopment: The baby's ears are developed enough to start detecting sounds from outside the womb — including your voice when you talk or sing to the bump. At about 5 inches long and 4 ounces, movements are increasing in both frequency and strength, though most are still too gentle to feel from outside the belly.
weeks.partnerExperience: The baby bump is becoming visibly noticeable to others, and back pain may begin as her center of gravity shifts forward. She may also feel the first faint flickers of movement this week — often described as a light tapping, bubbling, or fluttering sensation low in the abdomen.
howToHelp: Start talking to the bump — baby can hear you
Begin nursery planning and design
Help with back pain by offering massages

actionItems.text: Start planning the nursery layout and theme
Talk or sing to the baby bump

weeks.commonDadQuestion: Can the baby hear me yet?
weeks.commonDadAnswer: Not quite yet — hearing develops around week 18-20. But it's never too early to start. Babies recognize their parents' voices at birth, so building the habit now means you'll be comfortable doing it later.

weeks.title: Week 17: Vernix Coating Forms
weeks.babyDevelopment: A protective waxy coating called vernix caseosa has started forming on the baby's skin, shielding it from the constant exposure to amniotic fluid. The skeleton is undergoing a major transformation, with soft cartilage gradually hardening into bone throughout the body — a process called ossification that will continue well after birth.
weeks.partnerExperience: Increased vaginal discharge is a normal — if surprising — symptom at this stage, caused by hormonal changes and increased blood flow to the pelvic area. Many women feel their first recognizable baby movements around now, often described as a fluttering, bubbling, or popping sensation deep in the lower abdomen.
howToHelp: Talk and read to the bump daily
Help her stay comfortable with pillows and positioning
Research childbirth class options

actionItems.text: Read a book or tell a story to the bump
Look into childbirth class schedules

weeks.commonDadQuestion: Does talking to the belly really matter?
weeks.commonDadAnswer: Yes. Research shows babies recognize their parents' voices at birth. Talking now builds that bond and familiarizes the baby with your voice. Even if it feels awkward, keep at it.

weeks.title: Week 18: Baby Hears Sounds
weeks.babyDevelopment: The baby can now hear external sounds clearly — your voice, music, the ambient noise of everyday life. Unique fingerprints are fully formed, and movements are becoming more deliberate and frequent as muscle coordination improves. The baby can even respond to a sudden loud noise with a startled jump.
weeks.partnerExperience: First fetal movements — called quickening — become unmistakable for many women this week if they haven't already. She may describe the sensation as butterflies, gentle taps, or small bubbles moving around. Feeling the baby move for the first time is one of the most emotionally powerful milestones of the entire pregnancy.
howToHelp: Sing or play music to the bump
Put your hand on her belly and wait patiently for movement
Keep talking to the baby regularly

actionItems.text: Create a playlist to play for the baby
Register for a childbirth class

weeks.commonDadQuestion: When will I feel the baby kick?
weeks.commonDadAnswer: Partners typically feel kicks from outside around weeks 20-24, once movements get strong enough. Your partner may feel flutters earlier. Put your hand on her belly often — be patient, it's worth the wait.

weeks.title: Week 19: Unique Fingerprints
weeks.babyDevelopment: The baby's fingerprints are permanently set — the same unique pattern that will identify this person for their entire life. A regular sleep-wake cycle is developing, and sensory processing is accelerating as the brain forms specialized regions for touch, taste, smell, sight, and sound.
weeks.partnerExperience: Quickening — those now-recognizable baby movements — is likely a regular and exciting part of her day. The belly is growing visibly week by week, and feeling the baby move frequently often deepens the emotional bond between both parents and the baby in a way that nothing else quite does.
howToHelp: Try to feel the baby kick by placing your hand on her belly
Keep the nursery planning moving forward
Ask her what she needs most right now

actionItems.text: Try to feel baby movements together
Order key nursery furniture if not done yet

weeks.commonDadQuestion: Is sex still safe?
weeks.commonDadAnswer: For most uncomplicated pregnancies, yes — sex is safe throughout. Check with her OB if there's any specific concern. Positions may need to adjust as the belly grows. Check in with her regularly.

weeks.title: Week 20: Halfway There
weeks.babyDevelopment: Halfway point. The baby is now about 10 inches long — measured head to toe for the first time — and all five senses are actively developing. The anatomy scan at this milestone appointment gives a detailed look at every major organ and structure, checking that everything is developing as it should and often revealing the baby's sex.
weeks.partnerExperience: Kicks are now strong enough to feel clearly from outside the belly, and sometimes even visible as a ripple across the skin. Energy is usually good during this midpoint stretch, and many women say this week marks the start of feeling genuinely settled, connected, and at peace with the pregnancy.
howToHelp: Attend the anatomy scan — this is the big one
Discuss whether you want to find out the gender
Celebrate the halfway milestone

actionItems.text: Attend the 20-week anatomy scan
Celebrate hitting the halfway mark

weeks.commonDadQuestion: Should we find out the gender?
weeks.commonDadAnswer: Completely personal. Finding out can help with planning and bonding, but the surprise is special too. If you two disagree, talk it through — there's no wrong answer.

weeks.title: Week 21: Bone Marrow Active
weeks.babyDevelopment: The bone marrow is now producing blood cells, gradually taking over that role from the liver and spleen. The baby is becoming more active and responsive to sound — loud noises may produce a noticeable startle reaction. Movements are stronger and more intentional as muscle strength and coordination continue to develop.
weeks.partnerExperience: Stretch marks may begin appearing on the belly, hips, and breasts as the skin stretches to accommodate rapid growth. Applying belly oil or lotion can help with comfort and itchiness, though genetics plays the biggest role in whether stretch marks actually develop.
howToHelp: Offer belly massages with stretch mark oil or cocoa butter
Register for childbirth classes now
Keep encouraging her body confidence

actionItems.text: Register for a childbirth class
Pick up belly oil or lotion to help with stretch marks

weeks.commonDadQuestion: Why do I feel left out?
weeks.commonDadAnswer: This is one of the most common feelings dads report, and it makes sense — the physical experience is all hers. Stay involved: go to appointments, feel kicks, set up the nursery. Engagement is what matters.

weeks.title: Week 22: Baby Grabs Umbilical Cord
weeks.babyDevelopment: The baby is developed enough to grasp the umbilical cord with its tiny hands. Eyebrows and eyelashes are fully formed, and the lips are becoming more distinct and defined. The skin is still thin and somewhat translucent, but fat is beginning to accumulate beneath the surface, filling out the baby's appearance.
weeks.partnerExperience: Kicks are now strong and regular enough that you may be able to feel them clearly by placing your hand on her belly. She may also notice changes in skin pigmentation — such as the linea nigra, a dark line running down the center of the abdomen — caused by the hormonal changes of pregnancy.
howToHelp: Interview pediatricians early — good ones fill up fast
Continue talking and reading to the bump
Make sure the nursery progress is on track

actionItems.text: Research and interview potential pediatricians
Check in on nursery progress and order anything missing

weeks.commonDadQuestion: How do I choose a pediatrician?
weeks.commonDadAnswer: Ask your OB or friends for referrals. Many pediatricians offer free meet-and-greet visits before birth. Look for someone accepting new patients, close to home, with a communication style that works for you. Choose before week 36.

weeks.title: Week 23: Earliest Viability
weeks.babyDevelopment: This week marks the earliest viability milestone — if born now, the baby has a chance of survival with intensive neonatal medical care. The lungs are maturing but not yet capable of breathing independently; the next several weeks are critical for surfactant production and lung development.
weeks.partnerExperience: Braxton Hicks contractions — painless, practice tightening of the uterus — may start appearing and can be startling the first time they happen. She may also feel short of breath more easily now, as the growing uterus pushes upward against the diaphragm and limits how deeply she can inhale.
howToHelp: Schedule a hospital tour together
Start researching your birth hospital's policies
Reassure her about the Braxton Hicks — they're normal

actionItems.text: Schedule a hospital or birth center tour
Learn the difference between Braxton Hicks and real contractions

weeks.commonDadQuestion: What are Braxton Hicks?
weeks.commonDadAnswer: Practice contractions — the uterus tightening and releasing to prepare for labor. They're usually irregular and stop if she changes position or drinks water. Regular, painful contractions before week 37 should go to the OB.

weeks.title: Week 24: Lungs Structurally Complete
weeks.babyDevelopment: The lungs have developed all their essential structural components, though they're still not capable of breathing air independently. The baby's face is nearly fully formed, and unique footprints are developing — the same impressions that will be inked on the birth certificate the day this baby arrives.
weeks.partnerExperience: The glucose tolerance test typically happens around this week to screen for gestational diabetes — it involves drinking a sugary solution and having blood drawn afterward. Swelling in the hands, feet, and ankles may begin as blood volume peaks and the body retains more fluid.
howToHelp: Update your will and life insurance — now is the time
Drive her to the glucose test and keep her company
Start thinking about the hospital bag

actionItems.text: Update your will and review life insurance
Support her through the glucose screening test

weeks.commonDadQuestion: What if the baby comes early?
weeks.commonDadAnswer: Know the signs of preterm labor: regular contractions, pelvic pressure, or fluid leaking. If anything seems off, call the OB. By week 28+, outcomes are much better — every week in the womb matters.

weeks.title: Week 25: Nervous System Maturing
weeks.babyDevelopment: The nervous system is maturing rapidly, with nerve pathways connecting throughout the body and refining the baby's ability to respond to sensation. Fat is accumulating beneath the skin, which will be critical for regulating body temperature after birth. The baby may even be sucking its thumb — a reflex it has been quietly practicing.
weeks.partnerExperience: Heartburn and indigestion are increasing as the growing uterus presses upward against the stomach, reducing its capacity and pushing acid upward. Back pain and hip discomfort may make it difficult to get comfortable at night — a full-length pregnancy pillow can make a meaningful difference in how much rest she gets.
howToHelp: Finalize the baby registry
Help her get comfortable at night with a pregnancy pillow
Keep heartburn-friendly foods stocked

actionItems.text: Finalize and share the baby registry
Pick up a pregnancy pillow if you haven't already

weeks.commonDadQuestion: Is heartburn harmful to the baby?
weeks.commonDadAnswer: No — it's uncomfortable for her but doesn't affect the baby. The growing uterus pushes stomach acid up. Tums are generally safe (confirm with OB). Small meals and not eating before bed both help.

weeks.title: Week 26: Surfactant Production
weeks.babyDevelopment: The lungs have started producing surfactant — a substance that keeps the tiny air sacs from collapsing and is essential for breathing after birth. The eyes are beginning to open and close for the first time, and the baby can now detect light filtering through the abdominal wall.
weeks.partnerExperience: Swelling in the hands, feet, and ankles is increasingly common as blood volume reaches its peak and circulation slows under the weight of the pregnancy. Sleep is becoming harder to get — between the need for frequent bathroom trips, physical discomfort, and vivid pregnancy dreams, truly restful nights are getting rare.
howToHelp: Begin childcare interviews if you haven't started
Help reduce swelling with foot rubs and elevation
Take on extra household tasks to let her rest

actionItems.text: Begin interviewing childcare providers
Help reduce swelling with evening foot massages

weeks.commonDadQuestion: When should we start the daycare search?
weeks.commonDadAnswer: Start now. Quality infant care often has 6-12+ month waitlists. Visit centers, get on multiple lists, and factor the cost into your budget — infant care can run $1,500-3,000+/month depending on location.

weeks.title: Week 27: Eyes Open
weeks.babyDevelopment: The baby's eyes open for the first time this week, and they can detect light and shadow through the abdominal wall. Brain activity has increased significantly, with more complex patterns beginning to emerge. At about 15 inches long and nearly 2 pounds, growth continues at a steady and impressive pace.
weeks.partnerExperience: Shortness of breath may begin as the growing uterus presses up against the diaphragm, limiting how deeply she can breathe. She may also notice the baby's activity patterns more clearly now — more active at certain times of day, quieter at others — and that predictable rhythm becomes its own source of reassurance.
howToHelp: Complete the glucose screening if not done
Ask how you can help her breathe easier
Plan a babymoon or relaxing getaway if possible

actionItems.text: Ensure glucose screening is complete
Plan a relaxing babymoon weekend

weeks.commonDadQuestion: How much weight should she be gaining?
weeks.commonDadAnswer: For a normal pre-pregnancy BMI, the typical range is 25-35 lbs total — about 1 lb/week in the second and third trimesters. Her OB is tracking this. Your job is to support healthy eating, not comment on her body.

weeks.title: Week 28: Third Trimester Begins
weeks.babyDevelopment: The baby may begin turning head-down in preparation for delivery, though there's still room to move for several more weeks. Brain development is accelerating rapidly, and fat layers are building up beneath the skin — giving the baby the rounded, softer appearance it will have at birth.
weeks.partnerExperience: Back pain worsens as the belly grows heavier and the center of gravity continues to shift forward. Fatigue returns in full force in the third trimester, and anxiety about the birth and about becoming a parent often starts to intensify as the due date shifts from abstract to imminent.
howToHelp: Draft the birth plan together
Take the hospital tour if not done
Start childbirth classes

actionItems.text: Draft your birth plan with your partner
Complete the hospital tour

weeks.commonDadQuestion: What goes in a birth plan?
weeks.commonDadAnswer: A birth plan covers preferences like pain management, who's in the room, cord cutting, skin-to-skin contact, and feeding intentions. Keep it to one page, stay flexible, and review it with her OB in advance.

weeks.title: Week 29: Fat Accumulating
weeks.babyDevelopment: Fat accumulation is ramping up, giving the baby a softer, more newborn-like appearance. The bones are hardening throughout the body, but the skull remains deliberately flexible — designed so the baby can navigate the birth canal. Muscle development is accelerating too, contributing to stronger and more forceful kicks.
weeks.partnerExperience: Fatigue hits hard again in the third trimester — sleep is disrupted by discomfort and frequent bathroom trips, and the physical weight of the pregnancy takes a real toll on her energy. She may feel emotionally overwhelmed by how much there still is to do, and quietly taking things off her plate matters more than ever right now.
howToHelp: Attend childbirth classes together
Take on even more at home so she can rest
Talk about your fears and excitement openly

actionItems.text: Attend your first childbirth class
Make sure the nursery is nearly complete

weeks.commonDadQuestion: What happens in childbirth class?
weeks.commonDadAnswer: You'll learn what to expect during labor, comfort and breathing techniques, when to go to the hospital, and what happens after delivery. It's worth it — dads who attend feel significantly more prepared and confident.

weeks.title: Week 30: Packing Up
weeks.babyDevelopment: The baby's brain is entering a period of intense development, forming the folds and grooves that give it its distinctive appearance and dramatically increase its surface area. The baby can now regulate its own body temperature to some degree, and fingernails and toenails are fully grown — ready for their first trim shortly after birth.
weeks.partnerExperience: Shortness of breath and heartburn are near-constant companions as the uterus presses on the diaphragm and stomach simultaneously. Most physical activities require noticeably more effort now, and she may feel uncomfortable almost continuously — acknowledging that reality without trying to minimize it goes a long way.
howToHelp: Start packing the hospital bag
Install the car seat and get it inspected
Keep encouraging her — the finish line is in sight

actionItems.text: Start packing the hospital bag
Install the car seat and schedule a safety inspection

weeks.commonDadQuestion: How often should the baby kick?
weeks.commonDadAnswer: From week 28+, track kick counts: 10 movements within 2 hours, once a day after a meal. If she notices a significant decrease in movement at any point, call the OB right away. Don't wait and see.

weeks.title: Week 31: Rapid Brain Development
weeks.babyDevelopment: The brain and nervous system are nearly fully developed, with all five senses fully functional. The baby now sleeps about 90% of the time, cycling through REM sleep — which may be when the earliest dreams occur. Movements may feel different now as the baby grows larger and available space inside the womb diminishes.
weeks.partnerExperience: Braxton Hicks contractions may become more frequent and noticeably stronger. Fetal movement can feel different now too — less like distinct kicks and more like rolls, stretches, and sustained pressure as the baby runs out of room to move freely.
howToHelp: Finalize the birth plan
Review signs of labor together
Make sure the car seat is installed correctly

actionItems.text: Finalize and review the birth plan
Learn the signs of labor

weeks.commonDadQuestion: When should we have the bag packed?
weeks.commonDadAnswer: Have it ready by week 36. Pack in three categories: for her (comfort items, snacks, toiletries), for you (charger, snacks, change of clothes), and for baby (going-home outfit, installed car seat ready to go).

weeks.title: Week 32: Practicing Breathing
weeks.babyDevelopment: The baby is practicing breathing movements — inhaling and exhaling amniotic fluid rhythmically to strengthen the lungs and the muscles that will power every breath after birth. Toenails and fingernails are fully grown, and many babies are now positioned head-down in preparation for delivery.
weeks.partnerExperience: Extreme fatigue, persistent pelvic pressure, and frequent bathroom trips are the defining features of this stretch of the pregnancy. She needs more rest than ever, and even simple tasks can feel exhausting — reducing her load as much as possible is one of the most concrete ways you can support her right now.
howToHelp: Make sure the hospital bag is packed
Have the route to the hospital mapped out
Prepare a list of people to call when labor begins

actionItems.text: Finish packing the hospital bag
Map and drive the route to the hospital

weeks.commonDadQuestion: What's my role during labor?
weeks.commonDadAnswer: You're her advocate and anchor. Remind her she can do this, communicate her birth plan to nurses, keep her comfortable, and stay calm. You don't need to fix anything — your presence matters more than you know.

weeks.title: Week 33: Immune System Boosting
weeks.babyDevelopment: The baby is receiving a steady transfer of antibodies from mom through the placenta, building the immune system that will protect it in the early weeks of life outside the womb. The bones are hardening throughout the body, with one important exception — the skull stays deliberately pliable so the baby can navigate the birth canal during delivery.
weeks.partnerExperience: Sleep deprivation, persistent swelling, and near-constant physical discomfort define this stretch of the third trimester. She is carrying close to a full-term baby's weight and likely feeling it everywhere — in her back, hips, and feet. Both emotional support and tangible help at home are equally essential right now.
howToHelp: Handle as much at home as possible
Remind her how incredible she is
Start wrapping up things at work

actionItems.text: Start wrapping up work projects before paternity leave
Double-check the hospital bag is fully packed

weeks.commonDadQuestion: Will I be a good father?
weeks.commonDadAnswer: The fact that you're asking is a good sign. No dad feels fully ready. Good fathering isn't about being perfect — it's about showing up, being present, and learning as you go. You have what it takes.

weeks.title: Week 34: Eyes Adjusting to Light
weeks.babyDevelopment: The baby's pupils are now reactive to light — they dilate in darkness and constrict when exposed to brightness. Fat deposits continue to fill out the face and limbs, giving the baby a softer, rounder look. Nearly all organ systems are developed enough to support life outside the womb, and survival rates for babies born at this point are very high.
weeks.partnerExperience: The baby may begin to drop lower into the pelvis — a process called lightening — which can relieve pressure on the lungs and let her breathe more easily. The trade-off is increased pelvic pressure and discomfort with every step. Waddling becomes unavoidable, and even short walks may feel like a significant effort.
howToHelp: Confirm your paternity leave plan with HR
Pre-register at the hospital if available
Keep the mood at home calm and positive

actionItems.text: Pre-register at the hospital
Confirm your paternity leave paperwork is filed

weeks.commonDadQuestion: Are we actually ready?
weeks.commonDadAnswer: More than you think. The nursery doesn't need to be perfect, and you don't need every item on the registry. The essentials are love, safety, and presence — you can figure out everything else as you go.

weeks.title: Week 35: Almost Ready
weeks.babyDevelopment: The baby is nearly fully developed, with kidneys and liver fully functional and ready for life outside the womb. Most babies are in the head-down position by now, and the primary focus of these final weeks is weight gain and the last stages of lung maturation before birth.
weeks.partnerExperience: Frequent urination, pelvic pressure, and shortness of breath are the defining discomforts of this late stage. She is physically exhausted and emotionally right at the edge of the finish line — every twinge and pressure shift gets her full attention, and her patience for waiting is understandably very thin.
howToHelp: Know the signs of labor and when to go to the hospital
Keep her fed, hydrated, and rested
Be ready to leave for the hospital at any time

actionItems.text: Review labor signs and know when to head to the hospital
Make sure your phone is charged and car has gas at all times

weeks.commonDadQuestion: What do I pack for the hospital?
weeks.commonDadAnswer: For you: snacks (the cafeteria may be closed at 3am), phone charger, a change of clothes, and something for early labor downtime. Don't overpack — most of what you need is already at the hospital.

weeks.title: Week 36: Dropping Down
weeks.babyDevelopment: The baby is dropping lower into the pelvis in preparation for delivery. Fat continues to fill out the face and body, adding softness and weight — the baby is close to 6 pounds now and gaining about an ounce each day. The immune system is receiving its final boosts of antibodies transferred through the placenta.
weeks.partnerExperience: As the baby drops, she may find breathing a bit easier — a noticeable and welcome relief after weeks of feeling short of breath. The trade-off is a significant increase in pelvic pressure, and weekly prenatal appointments now begin to monitor for signs that labor is approaching.
howToHelp: Attend weekly prenatal appointments with her
Finalize all baby gear and nursery setup
Make a plan for who watches any older kids or pets

actionItems.text: Finalize nursery and make sure everything is set up
Arrange care for pets or older children during delivery

weeks.commonDadQuestion: How do I install the car seat?
weeks.commonDadAnswer: Read the manual and use either the LATCH system or the seatbelt — not both. The seat should not move more than 1 inch side to side. Many fire stations offer free inspections. Get it checked before the due date.

weeks.title: Week 37: Early Full Term
weeks.babyDevelopment: The baby is officially considered early full term — all organs are ready and functioning. These final weeks are primarily about weight gain and the last fine-tuning of the lungs, with the baby adding about half a pound per week. Every additional day in the womb is meaningful for brain and lung development.
weeks.partnerExperience: The nesting instinct often kicks in powerfully this week — a sudden, intense urge to clean, organize, rearrange, and prepare every corner of the home. Support it, lean in, and help wherever she directs you. It's the brain's way of getting ready, and it can be a surprisingly joyful shared experience.
howToHelp: Help with any nesting projects
Go over the birth plan one more time
Stay close to home and reachable

actionItems.text: Review the birth plan together one final time
Stay reachable — keep your phone on at all times

weeks.commonDadQuestion: What are the signs of real labor?
weeks.commonDadAnswer: Regular contractions that get closer together, stronger, and longer — unlike Braxton Hicks, they don't stop with movement or water. Other signs: water breaking, bloody show. When in doubt, call the OB.

weeks.title: Week 38: Final Preparations
weeks.babyDevelopment: The brain and lungs continue their final maturation, making subtle but important improvements each day even at this late stage. The vernix coating is being shed and swallowed as the baby moves, and the lanugo — the fine hair that covered the body — is mostly gone. The baby is ready in every meaningful way.
weeks.partnerExperience: Anxiety and anticipation are at a peak — every cramp, twinge, or shift in pressure feels like it could be the start of labor. She may swing between eager readiness for it all to be over and genuine nervousness about what lies ahead. Steady, calm reassurance is exactly what she needs most from you right now.
howToHelp: Be calm and reassuring — she needs your steadiness
Keep the hospital bag by the door
Have your contact list ready

actionItems.text: Place the hospital bag by the front door
Prepare a list of people to call or text after delivery

weeks.commonDadQuestion: When do we go to the hospital?
weeks.commonDadAnswer: For first-time parents, follow the 5-1-1 rule: contractions every 5 minutes, lasting 1 minute, for 1 hour. If her water breaks, go in immediately. Always call the OB or hospital first — they'll confirm when to come.

weeks.title: Week 39: Full Term
weeks.babyDevelopment: Full term. The baby is fully developed and ready for birth at any moment. The lungs have reached complete maturity and are prepared to take that first breath of air. At around 7 pounds and 20 inches, the baby has everything it needs — now it's just a matter of timing.
weeks.partnerExperience: She is likely very uncomfortable, very tired, and very ready for this pregnancy to be over. Distinguishing Braxton Hicks from real labor is a constant mental exercise, and every contraction gets her full attention. Your calmness, your availability, and your steady presence are the most important things you can offer her right now.
howToHelp: Don't leave her side for long
Keep the car fueled up
Practice your breathing techniques together

actionItems.text: Practice breathing and labor support techniques
Keep the car gassed up and ready

weeks.commonDadQuestion: What if she goes past the due date?
weeks.commonDadAnswer: It's common — only about 5% of babies arrive on their due date. Most OBs will induce by 41-42 weeks. Keep her comfortable, stay close to home, and make sure your bag is packed and car seat is installed.

weeks.title: Week 40: Game Day
weeks.babyDevelopment: The baby is fully developed — typically 18 to 20 inches long and around 7 to 8 pounds — and ready to enter the world at any moment. The placenta is still actively delivering nutrients and antibodies. Everything that has been building over the past 40 weeks has been leading to this single moment.
weeks.partnerExperience: She is at or past her due date — exhausted, anxious, and more than ready. This is one of the hardest waiting periods of the entire pregnancy, when time seems to slow to a crawl. Your job is simple but essential: stay present, stay calm, and be her rock through whatever comes next.
howToHelp: Stay close and keep your phone on
Be calm — she needs your energy to be steady
Remind her she's almost there

actionItems.text: Keep your phone fully charged at all times
Review the 5-1-1 rule for when to go to the hospital

weeks.commonDadQuestion: What do I do when labor starts?
weeks.commonDadAnswer: Stay calm, time the contractions, and call the OB or hospital when contractions follow the 5-1-1 pattern. Grab the bag, help her to the car, and keep reassuring her. You've prepared for this — trust yourself.
